title: Partial Application
body:
In [[Haskell]] **every function takes exactly one argument.** A function that appears to take
two is a function of one argument that returns a function of one argument, so `f x y` parses as
`(f x) y`. That is **currying**, named for Haskell Curry, and it is inherited directly from
[[Lambda Calculus]], where $\lambda x. \lambda y. M$ is the only way to have two parameters.

**Partial application** is what currying buys: supply fewer arguments than the function
"takes" and you get back a function waiting for the rest.

```haskell
add :: Int -> Int -> Int      -- really Int -> (Int -> Int)
add x y = x + y

add 3      :: Int -> Int      -- a new function, not an error
increment  = add 1
map (add 10) [1, 2, 3]        -- [11, 12, 13]
```

Read the arrow as right-associative and the type signature stops being mysterious:
`Int -> Int -> Int` *is* `Int -> (Int -> Int)`. This is why Haskell writes types with arrows
instead of a parameter list; the notation is telling you the truth about the language.

## Sections

Operators partially apply too, by wrapping in parentheses:

```haskell
(* 2)      -- \x -> x * 2
(2 ^)      -- \x -> 2 ^ x
(subtract 3)   -- (- 3) would parse as negative three
map (* 2) [1, 2, 3]        -- [2, 4, 6]
filter (> 5) [3, 7, 2, 9]  -- [7, 9]
```

The `(- 3)` exception is the one that catches people, and it is a lexical accident rather than
a deep fact.

## Point-free style

Because a partially applied function is just a value, you can define functions by combining
others without ever naming the argument:

```haskell
sumOfSquares = sum . map (^ 2)     -- (.) is composition
countEvens   = length . filter even
```

`f . g` is $\lambda x.\, f(g(x))$, the composition from [[Category Theory]], and it is an
operator here rather than a notation. Point-free code is shorter and reads as a pipeline; taken
too far it becomes unreadable, which is why it is affectionately called point-*less* style.

## Against the languages you already know

| Language | How multiple arguments work | Partial application |
|---|---|---|
| [[C]] | a fixed parameter list, all or nothing | impossible |
| [[Java]] | same, plus [[Overloading\|overloads]] by arity | no; you write another method |
| [[JavaScript]] | fixed list, but functions are values | possible by hand: `const add1 = y => add(1, y)`, or `bind` |
| [[Haskell]] | one argument, always | the default; nothing special is happening |

The JavaScript row is the useful comparison, because [[Closure]] is exactly the mechanism.
`add 1` in Haskell is a closure over `x = 1`; the difference is that Haskell builds it for you
every time rather than making you write the wrapper. See [[Arrow Syntax]] and
[[Anonymous Function]] for how the same idea reads in JS.

## Core Facts to Know

- Every Haskell function takes one argument; `f x y` means `(f x) y`.
- **Currying**: multiple arguments as nested one-argument functions, from [[Lambda Calculus]].
- `->` in a type is right-associative: `a -> b -> c` is `a -> (b -> c)`.
- **Partial application**: supplying fewer arguments returns a function, not an error.
- Operator **sections**: `(* 2)`, `(> 5)`, `(2 ^)`. `(- 3)` is negative three, use `subtract`.
- The partially applied function is a [[Closure]] over the arguments given so far.
- `.` is function composition; **point-free** style defines functions without naming arguments.
- Argument order in a signature is a design decision: put the data last so sections read well.
